parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A bar magnet is released above a stationary conducting loop connected to a high-resistance voltmeter. As the magnet approaches, the magnetic flux through the loop changes. Explain why the voltmeter gives a reading, referring to Faraday’s law.

answer.text: The changing flux induces an emf around the loop. For one turn, ε=−dΦ/dt, so the voltmeter registers a voltage while the flux changes. Its magnitude depends on the rate of flux change, not simply on the size of the flux; the sign depends on the chosen lead polarity.

parts.display_text: The graph shows magnetic flux Φ through a single loop as a magnet falls through it. Estimate the maximum magnitude of the induced emf. The flux axis is in kg m² s⁻² A⁻¹, equivalent to webers.

answer.text: For one turn, |ε|=|dΦ/dt|. Draw a tangent where the falling branch is steepest, near t≈0.38 s, and calculate its gradient. A representative tangent gives a change of about 0.09 Wb in about 0.06 s, so the maximum magnitude is approximately 1.5 V. Reasonable tangent choices on this scanned graph give about 1.3–1.6 V.

parts.display_text: A bar magnet falls vertically through a closed horizontal conducting loop, with its north pole downward. State the induced conventional-current direction as the magnet enters and as it leaves, both as viewed from above.

answer.text: Entering: anticlockwise as viewed from above, producing an upward field to oppose the increasing downward flux. Leaving: clockwise, producing a downward field to oppose the decreasing downward flux.

parts.display_text: A small coil is moved along the central axis inside a long solenoid carrying constant current. Throughout the motion the magnetic field is uniform and parallel to the coil’s area normal. Describe the flux linkage as the coil moves, and state whether this motion induces an emf.

answer.text: Flux linkage NΦ = NBA remains constant because N, B, A and the orientation are constant. No emf is induced, since the flux linkage does not change.

parts.display_text: A fixed coil has its area normal parallel to a uniform field. The field stays at 0.040 T from time 0 to t₀, rises linearly to 0.080 T at 2t₀, then falls linearly to zero at 4t₀. Sketch the induced emf against time from 0 to 4t₀, taking increasing flux as positive.

answer.text: The emf is zero from 0 to t₀. It is a constant negative value from t₀ to 2t₀ and a constant positive value of equal magnitude from 2t₀ to 4t₀. The magnitude is NA(0.040 T)/t₀.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
A conducting bar of length ℓ slides at constant speed v along conducting rails, completing a loop in a uniform field B perpendicular to the loop. The bar’s resistance is R; other resistances are negligible. The induced current is I = ε/R and the magnetic force magnitude is F = BIℓ. What magnetic force magnitude acts on the moving bar?

A. Bℓv/R
B. B²ℓ²v/R
C. Bv/R
D. B²ℓv/R

answer.text: B. The induced emf is ε = Bℓv. Substituting into the supplied relations gives F = Bℓ(ε/R) = B²ℓ²v/R. The force opposes the motion.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Half of a stationary circular loop of radius r lies in a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. Over time Δt the field increases uniformly from B₀ to 4B₀. Derive the magnitude of the induced emf and determine the direction of current around the loop.

answer.text: Only area πr²/2 is within the field. |ε| = |ΔΦ|/Δt = (πr²/2)(3B₀/Δt) = 3πr²B₀/(2Δt). The increasing into-page flux induces an out-of-page field, requiring an anticlockwise current.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A circular conducting loop is pulled across a straight boundary into a region of uniform magnetic field perpendicular to its plane. The field is constant in time. Explain whether an emf is induced (a) while the loop is entering the region and (b) while it continues moving wholly within the region.

answer.text: (a) Yes. The area of the loop inside the field increases, so its flux changes. (b) No. Once wholly inside, the field, enclosed area and orientation are constant, so the flux is constant despite the motion.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: State Faraday’s law of electromagnetic induction.

answer.text: The induced emf is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage. With SI definitions, ε = −d(NΦ)/dt; the minus sign expresses the direction opposing the change.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text:
A conducting rod of length l moves to the right, perpendicular to its length and to a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. It starts from rest with constant acceleration a, so its speed is v = at. Its induced-emf magnitude is plotted against time.

(a) Explain how the graph supports emf proportional to speed.
(b) Use the rate of magnetic flux swept out to show ε = Blat.
(c) Determine B when l = 0.45 m and a = 7.8 m s⁻².

answer.text:
(a) The emf–time graph is a straight line through the origin, and v = at means speed is proportional to time; therefore emf is proportional to speed.
(b) In a short interval dt the rod sweeps area dA = lv dt. The flux change associated with this swept area is dΦ = B dA, so |ε| = dΦ/dt = Blv = Blat.
(c) The graph gives ε = 0.30 mV at t = 2.0 s. B = (0.30 × 10⁻³)/(0.45 × 7.8 × 2.0) = 4.27 × 10⁻⁵ T ≈ 4.3 × 10⁻⁵ T.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: An ohmic bulb of resistance R forms part of a conducting loop of area A perpendicular to the magnetic field. The source field is constant at +B₁ before t₁, falls linearly to −B₁ at t₃, and then remains constant. Graph 3 gives cumulative energy dissipated since t=0. (b) Explain how this graph changes if only bulb resistance increases. (c) With the original bulb the field instead falls from +2B₁ to −2B₁ in the same interval: explain the graph change. (d) A student proposes E=A²B₁R/[4(t₃−t₁)]. Whether or not that full equation is correct, assess whether its inverse dependence on Δt=t₃−t₁ makes physical sense.

answer.text: The induced emf magnitude A|ΔB|/Δt is unchanged when only R increases; P=ε²/R falls, so cumulative energy rises with a smaller slope and ends lower. Doubling |ΔB| doubles ε and makes P four times larger, so the slope and final energy are four times larger. Since ε∝1/Δt, P∝1/Δt² and E=PΔt∝1/Δt, the inverse time dependence is physically sensible for fixed ΔB. The displayed full expression is dimensionally wrong and also puts R in the wrong proportionality; only the requested time dependence is supported. Cumulative energy remains zero before t₁ and constant after t₃ in both comparisons, since flux does not change outside that interval.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: A rectangular conducting loop moves right at constant speed into a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. The source figure shows positions at t₁, t₂ and t₃. Compare the magnitude and direction of current at these times, explaining whether magnetic flux changes.

answer.text: At t₁ and t₂ the overlap area changes at equal rates, so induced currents have equal nonzero magnitudes. They flow anticlockwise for the source orientations because Lenz’s law makes the induced field oppose the corresponding flux change. At t₃ the loop is wholly within a uniform field, flux is constant, and no current flows.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: The source shows two concentric wire loops. The outer loop has a battery and open switch; the inner loop is closed. What current appears in the inner loop when the switch is closed? A. steady clockwise  B. steady anticlockwise  C. momentary clockwise  D. momentary anticlockwise

answer.text: C. The source battery orientation makes the outer current anticlockwise, so its growing field is out of the page. Lenz’s law gives a momentary clockwise inner current whose field opposes that increase. Once the outer current is steady, flux is constant and induced current is zero. The official report key C is correct; its prose saying 'anticlockwise' is a typographical inconsistency resolved from the source diagram.

parts.label: whole
parts.display_text: Editorial adaptation: A 200-turn coil is initially in the position shown and rotates at 60 Hz in a 5.0 mT field. Its average induced emf during the first quarter-turn is 35 mV. You are given that the generator’s commutator makes the displayed output voltage equal to the magnitude |emf| of the signed coil emf, with the same output polarity on every half-turn. The supplied graph shows this output voltage. (a) State the current direction in the coil, viewed from above, during the first quarter-turn. (b) Calculate the area of one loop. (c) On the same axes, sketch the output voltage for 100 turns and 30 Hz.

answer.text: Official report checked; editorial worked explanation: (a) the magnetic field runs from the N pole to the S pole. Applying the generator right-hand rule to the shown direction of conductor motion gives a clockwise conventional current when viewed from above; the induced current opposes the flux change. (b) During the first quarter-turn the magnitude of the flux-linkage change is NBA, from zero to maximum magnitude, so Δt=1/(4f)=1/240 s and A=εΔt/(NB)=1.46×10⁻⁴ m². (c) The rectified output amplitude scales with Nf, becoming one quarter, while halving rotation frequency doubles the pulse period.

original-ib26mb2-written-9-bii:whole.hint: Faraday’s law relates induced emf to a rate of change. Identify what changes even though the loop itself is stationary.
notes: Relative motion of the magnet can change the flux through a stationary loop. It is not necessary for the wire itself to move.
A high-resistance voltmeter can measure induced emf with negligible current. Do not infer a substantial current merely from a voltage reading.

original-ib26mb2-written-9-ci:whole.hint: Look for the greatest magnitude of gradient, not the highest point of the flux curve.
notes: At maximum flux the gradient is zero, so the instantaneous emf is zero there. The largest emf occurs on the steeper side of the pulse.
Use a tangent and two well-separated points on that tangent. Dividing maximum flux by the entire pulse duration gives an average rate, not the maximum.

original-ib26mb2-written-9-cii:whole.hint: Determine whether the downward magnetic flux is increasing or decreasing, then use Lenz’s law and the right-hand grip rule.
notes: The induced field opposes the change in flux, not always the original field. This explains why the current reverses after the magnet passes through.
Clockwise and anticlockwise require a stated viewpoint. The closed-loop condition is needed for an induced current; an open circuit can have emf without a sustained current.

cross-vc23-5:whole.hint: Look for a change in magnetic flux linkage, not just the presence of a magnetic field.
notes: Magnetic flux is Φ = BA cos θ for a uniform field, with θ measured from the surface normal. Faraday’s law is ε = −N dΦ/dt.
A changing field, area or orientation can induce an emf. On a flux–time graph use the gradient; a large constant flux by itself gives no emf.

cross-vc23-6:whole.hint: Read whether the question asks for flux or flux linkage.
notes: Flux through one loop is Φ = BA cosθ, using the angle to the area normal. Flux linkage is NΦ; multiplying by the number of turns answers a different question here.
For a circular coil A = πr². Convert the radius from centimetres to metres before squaring.
